Welcome to 6th Grade Digital Discoveries

CPALMS #0200021 Florida CS Standards SC.6.*

Optima Academy Online — Grade 6 Digital Discoveries (CPALMS #0200021). An asynchronous, self-paced computer science course aligned to Florida Computer Science Standards (SC.6.*). Students explore digital communication, data and cyber safety, programming with Python, modeling and AI ethics, and complete a year-end capstone project.

What you'll learn this year

Across five units and 36 weeks, you'll move from everyday digital communication into the fundamentals of programming, modeling, and AI ethics — finishing with a year-end capstone where you put it all together.

Course flow

  • Unit 1 — Digital Foundations — Weeks 1–7. Digital communication, multimedia, file organization, productivity tools.
  • Unit 2 — Data & Cyber Safety — Weeks 9–18. The journey of data, permissions, phishing, encryption, source evaluation, and digital wellness.
  • Unit 3 — Programming — Weeks 19–28. Computational thinking, flowcharts, Python data types, conditionals, loops, functions, debugging.
  • Unit 4 — Modeling, Design & AI — Weeks 29–33. Simulation, the engineering design process, AI fundamentals, ethics, and human-AI collaboration.
  • Unit 5 — Capstone & Course Final — Weeks 35–36. Careers in computing, year-end capstone project, and course final.

How each week works

  • Reading — the concept page introducing the week's topic and vocabulary.
  • Activity — an interactive practice task (scenarios, sorting, decision-making) that reinforces the reading.
  • Quiz — 5 multiple-choice questions, 3 attempts, instant feedback. Best attempt is kept.

At the end of each unit, a longer summative Unit Assessment checks your mastery. Unit 5 ends with the cumulative Course Final.

Getting started

  1. Click Modules in the left sidebar — that's the main navigation for this course.
  2. Open the Course Syllabus page (in the Start Here module) to see the full week-by-week plan.
  3. Start with Unit 1, Week 1 and complete each week's reading → activity → quiz in order.

quizzes.title: Week 19 Quiz — Introduction to Computational Thinking

questions.text: Which of the following BEST describes computational thinking?

answers.text: A way to fix broken computers and replace hardware parts
answers.feedback: ❌ That's computer repair. Computational thinking is a way of thinking about problems, not a hardware skill.

answers.text: A method for solving problems by decomposing them, finding patterns, abstracting essentials, and writing clear steps
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Computational thinking is the four-pillar problem-solving toolkit — decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design — that works in any language. (SC.K12.CTR.1.1)

answers.text: Memorizing the rules of a programming language like Python
answers.feedback: ❌ Memorizing language rules is just one small part of programming. Computational thinking is broader — it works before you ever pick a language.

answers.text: Building physical computer hardware in a workshop
answers.feedback: ❌ Hardware engineering is its own field. Computational thinking is about problem-solving, not building physical machines.

questions.text: Which scenario shows decomposition at work?

answers.text: Asking your friend to do the entire research project for you
answers.feedback: ❌ That's delegation, not decomposition. The big problem hasn't been broken down into smaller parts — it's just been handed off.

answers.text: Splitting a research project into smaller jobs: pick a topic, gather sources, write a draft, edit, format
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! One big problem becomes five smaller ones, each one easy to start. That's textbook decomposition. (SC.K12.CTR.1.1)

answers.text: Writing a long paragraph about the topic without stopping
answers.feedback: ❌ Writing without stopping isn't breaking the problem down — it's just diving in. There are no smaller pieces identified.

answers.text: Reading a textbook from front to back without taking notes
answers.feedback: ❌ Reading is gathering information, not breaking the project into parts. No decomposition happened.

questions.text: Why is pattern recognition so useful in computer science?

answers.text: It lets you reuse a solution that already works on similar problems
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Once you've spotted the pattern in a problem, you can reuse the same shape of solution on every similar problem you meet. That saves time and reduces mistakes. (SC.K12.CTR.2.1)

answers.text: It makes the computer's processor physically faster
answers.feedback: ❌ Pattern recognition is a thinking skill, not a hardware upgrade. Processor speed is a separate physical thing.

answers.text: It removes the need to ever write algorithms
answers.feedback: ❌ Pattern recognition helps us write algorithms — it doesn't replace them. You still need clear, ordered steps.

answers.text: It hides the bugs in your code so they don't show up
answers.feedback: ❌ Pattern recognition has nothing to do with hiding bugs. We track bugs by debugging — a different skill (Week 26!).

questions.text: Which of these is the BEST example of abstraction?

answers.text: A video game that includes every detail of a real city — every leaf, brick, and stoplight
answers.feedback: ❌ That's the opposite of abstraction — that's keeping every detail. Abstraction throws unimportant details away.

answers.text: A subway map that shows only the stations and lines, not the real distances or curves
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A subway map is the classic example of abstraction: it keeps the details that matter (lines and stops) and drops the ones that don't (real distances, curves). (SC.K12.CTR.5.1)

answers.text: Counting every single leaf on a tree before drawing it
answers.feedback: ❌ Counting every leaf is keeping all the details. Abstraction would be drawing the tree as a green blob and a brown trunk.

answers.text: Memorizing every fact about every classmate before a test
answers.feedback: ❌ Memorizing everything is the opposite of abstraction. Abstraction means keeping only what matters for this task.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a required trait of an algorithm?

answers.text: It eventually stops — it is finite
answers.feedback: ❌ Being finite IS a required trait — an algorithm must eventually stop. So this is a real trait, not the answer.

answers.text: It has clear, ordered steps
answers.feedback: ❌ Clear ordered steps ARE a required trait of every algorithm. So this is a real trait, not the answer.

answers.text: It must be written in the Python programming language
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Algorithms are language-independent — you can write the same algorithm as plain steps, in pseudocode, in Python, in JavaScript, or in any other language. The language is just how we express the algorithm. (SC.K12.CTR.1.1)

answers.text: It produces an output (an answer, a result, or an action)
answers.feedback: ❌ Producing an output IS a required trait. So this is a real trait, not the answer.

questions.text: Which flowchart shape marks the START or END of an algorithm?

answers.text: Rectangle
answers.feedback: ❌ Rectangles are for process steps (calculations, actions). Not for marking start or end.

answers.text: Diamond
answers.feedback: ❌ Diamonds ask yes/no questions and split the path. Not for start or end.

answers.text: Oval (terminator)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The oval (also called a "terminator") is the only shape used for START and END. (SC.K12.CTR.1.1)

answers.text: Parallelogram
answers.feedback: ❌ Parallelograms are for getting input or showing output. Not for start or end.

questions.text: What is a diamond shape used for in a flowchart?

answers.text: Showing information to the user (output)
answers.feedback: ❌ Output is the parallelogram's job (Input/Output shape). The diamond does something different.

answers.text: Marking the start of the program
answers.feedback: ❌ Starting the program is the oval's job (terminator). Not the diamond.

answers.text: Connecting two arrows together
answers.feedback: ❌ Plain arrows connect shapes together — diamonds are not connectors.

answers.text: Asking a yes/no question that splits the path
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Every diamond holds a yes/no question. It always has TWO arrows leaving — one for YES, one for NO. (SC.K12.CTR.2.1)

questions.text: How many arrows should leave a single decision diamond?

answers.text: Exactly two — one for YES, one for NO
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A diamond ALWAYS has exactly two arrows leaving — labeled YES and NO. That's what makes it a "decision." (SC.K12.CTR.2.1)

answers.text: Exactly one — flowcharts always have a single path
answers.feedback: ❌ Flowcharts can branch — that's the whole point of a diamond. One outgoing arrow would mean no decision.

answers.text: Three or more, one for each possible answer
answers.feedback: ❌ A diamond is for yes/no questions only — that means exactly two outcomes.

answers.text: None — the diamond only receives arrows
answers.feedback: ❌ Diamonds receive AND send arrows. Without outgoing arrows the flow would dead-end at the question.

questions.text:
You're translating this pseudocode to a flowchart:

IF temperature > 80 THEN
    PRINT "It's hot!"

How many shapes (besides terminators and arrows) does this need?

answers.text: Just one — only the IF
answers.feedback: ❌ The PRINT is a separate step — it shows up only on the YES branch and needs its own shape.

answers.text: Two — a diamond for the IF and a parallelogram for the PRINT
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! One diamond for the IF condition, one parallelogram for the PRINT (output). Each step needs its matching shape. (SC.K12.CTR.3.1)

answers.text: Three — two diamonds and one rectangle
answers.feedback: ❌ There's only ONE decision here ("temperature > 80?"), not two. And a PRINT is a parallelogram, not a rectangle.

answers.text: None — pseudocode and flowcharts can't be translated
answers.feedback: ❌ Pseudocode and flowcharts ARE translatable — they describe the same algorithm in different forms.

questions.text: Why does every flowchart need a terminator (oval) at the start AND at the end?

answers.text: Because flowcharts crash without ovals
answers.feedback: ❌ Flowcharts don't "crash" — they're pictures, not running programs. The reason is about clarity.

answers.text: Because Canvas requires it as a file format
answers.feedback: ❌ Canvas doesn't enforce flowchart shapes. The convention exists because it makes charts readable.

answers.text: Because terminators show where to begin reading the chart and where the algorithm ends
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Without START and END terminators, a reader has no idea where the algorithm begins or finishes. Terminators are the bookends of every flowchart. (SC.K12.CTR.1.1)

answers.text: Because diamonds need ovals to work properly
answers.feedback: ❌ Diamonds work fine on their own — they don't depend on ovals. Terminators serve a different role: marking begin/end.

quizzes.title: Week 21 Quiz — Python Basics: Data Types & Variables

questions.text: In Python, what is a variable?

answers.text: A math problem the computer has to solve
answers.feedback: ❌ Variables don't run calculations on their own — they store values for later use.

answers.text: A labeled box that stores a value the program can use later
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A variable is a name (the label) attached to a value (the contents). The contents can change as the program runs. (SC.6.PE.1.1)

answers.text: A built-in Python function for printing text
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes print(), not a variable.

answers.text: Another word for a comment in the code
answers.feedback: ❌ Comments start with # and are ignored by Python — that's not a variable.

questions.text: In Python, what does the assignment operator (=) do?

answers.text: It checks whether two values are equal
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes the equality operator, written ==. The single = is different.

answers.text: It performs subtraction
answers.feedback: ❌ Subtraction uses the - operator. The = sign isn't math.

answers.text: It stores the value on the right into the variable on the left
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Read = as "gets the value of." score = 10 means "the variable score gets the value 10." (SC.6.PE.1.1)

answers.text: It deletes the variable
answers.feedback: ❌ Python doesn't delete a variable just by writing =. The del keyword is for that — but you don't need it yet.

questions.text: What data type is the literal value "3.14" in Python? (Pay close attention to the quotes!)

answers.text: float
answers.feedback: ❌ Without quotes, 3.14 would be a float. With quotes, it's text — Python doesn't peek inside the quotes to check.

answers.text: int
answers.feedback: ❌ ints are whole numbers. "3.14" has a decimal point AND is wrapped in quotes — neither fits int.

answers.text: string (str)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Anything wrapped in quotes is a string, even if the characters inside happen to look like a number. (SC.6.PE.1.1)

answers.text: bool
answers.feedback: ❌ Booleans only hold True or False. "3.14" is neither.

questions.text:
Python runs:

x = "Code"
y = "Quest"
print(x + y)

What appears on the screen?

answers.text: CodeQuest
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! When + is used between two strings, Python concatenates them — sticks them end-to-end with no space. The result is a string. (SC.6.PE.1.1)

answers.text: Code Quest (with a space between)
answers.feedback: ❌ Python doesn't add a space when you use +. The strings join exactly as they are.

answers.text: An error — you can't add strings
answers.feedback: ❌ You can! For strings, + means "join together" rather than "add up numerically."

answers.text: Code+Quest
answers.feedback: ❌ The + is the instruction, not part of the result. It disappears when Python builds the joined string.

questions.text: Why do programmers use descriptive variable names like high_score instead of single letters like x?

answers.text: Python runs descriptive names faster
answers.feedback: ❌ Variable names don't change how fast the code runs. Python treats x and high_score the same speed-wise.

answers.text: Single-letter names break the assignment operator
answers.feedback: ❌ Single letters like x are perfectly LEGAL in Python — they're just hard for humans to read.

answers.text: Descriptive names make code easier to read and understand later for yourself and others
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Code is read way more often than it's written. A name like high_score tells future-you (and your teammates) exactly what's in the box. (SC.6.PE.1.1)

answers.text: Python won't accept variable names shorter than three letters
answers.feedback: ❌ Python is fine with one-letter names. The community just discourages them because they're unclear.

questions.text: In pseudocode, what is the difference between == and =?

answers.text: They mean the same thing — both compare two values.
== compares two values (asks "are they equal?"); = assigns a value (sets a variable).
= compares two values; == assigns a value.
== is only used for text; = is only used for numbers.

questions.text:
Given age = 15, which branch of this code runs?

IF age >= 16 THEN
    PRINT "can drive"
ELSE
    PRINT "too young"
END IF

answers.text: The IF branch runs — prints "can drive".
Both branches run, one after the other.
The ELSE branch runs — prints "too young".
Neither branch runs because 15 doesn't equal 16.

questions.text:
Given n = 50, what does this code print?

IF n > 100 THEN
    PRINT "huge"
ELIF n > 10 THEN
    PRINT "medium"
ELSE
    PRINT "small"
END IF

answers.text: "huge"
"medium"
"small"
Both "medium" and "small"

questions.text: Why is ELIF useful instead of writing many separate IF statements?

answers.text: ELIF is faster — it skips to the answer instantly.
ELIF lets you check more conditions than IF allows.
ELIF works even when conditions overlap, but separate IFs do not.
With ELIF, only the first true branch runs and the rest are skipped — separate IFs would each be checked and could all run.

questions.text: Which of the following BEST describes computational thinking?

answers.text: Memorizing programming languages like Python
answers.feedback: ❌ CT is a way of thinking about problems, not memorization of any language.

answers.text: A four-pillar approach: decompose problems, find patterns, abstract essentials, and write algorithms
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The four pillars of CT — decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design — work together on any problem.

answers.text: Building computer hardware in a workshop
answers.feedback: ❌ Hardware is engineering. CT is about problem-solving, not building physical machines.

answers.text: Writing perfect code with no bugs the first time
answers.feedback: ❌ Even great programmers write bugs. CT helps you think clearly — bug-free isn't the goal.

questions.text: You've been asked to plan a multi-day school field trip. Which choice shows the BEST use of decomposition?

answers.text: Ask one teacher to handle every detail
answers.feedback: ❌ That's delegation, not decomposition. The big problem hasn't been broken down into pieces.

answers.text: Split the trip into sub-problems: transportation, food, lodging, activities, safety
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! One big problem becomes five smaller, solvable problems. That's decomposition. (SC.K12.CTR.1.1)

answers.text: Brainstorm randomly without any structure
answers.feedback: ❌ Random brainstorming isn't decomposition — there's no structure or breakdown.

answers.text: Just show up and improvise
answers.feedback: ❌ Improvising is the OPPOSITE of decomposition. No problem-breakdown happened.

questions.text: A streaming app shows you "you might also like..." recommendations. Which CT pillar is the app most relying on?

answers.text: Decomposition
answers.feedback: ❌ Decomposition is breaking a problem into parts. Recommendations are about spotting similarities.

answers.text: Pattern recognition
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The app finds patterns in your viewing history and matches them to other users' patterns. (SC.K12.CTR.2.1)

answers.text: Abstraction
answers.feedback: ❌ Abstraction is hiding details. Here, the app is matching shapes — that's pattern recognition.

answers.text: Algorithm finite-ness
answers.feedback: ❌ Finite-ness is a TRAIT of algorithms, not a pillar of CT.

questions.text: Which flowchart shape is used for both the START and the END of an algorithm?

answers.text: Diamond
answers.feedback: ❌ Diamonds ask yes/no questions and split the path. Not for start or end.

answers.text: Rectangle
answers.feedback: ❌ Rectangles are for process steps (calculations, actions). Not start or end.

answers.text: Oval (terminator)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The oval (terminator) is the only shape used for START and END. (SC.K12.CTR.1.1)

answers.text: Parallelogram
answers.feedback: ❌ Parallelograms are for input or output — not start or end.

questions.text: A correctly drawn decision diamond in a flowchart MUST have:

answers.text: Exactly one outgoing arrow
answers.feedback: ❌ One outgoing arrow means no decision happened. The diamond exists to SPLIT the path.

answers.text: Exactly two outgoing arrows, labeled YES and NO
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Diamonds are yes/no — exactly two paths out, one for YES and one for NO. (SC.K12.CTR.2.1)

answers.text: Three or more outgoing arrows
answers.feedback: ❌ A diamond is for yes/no only — exactly two outcomes.

answers.text: No outgoing arrows; only incoming ones
answers.feedback: ❌ Without outgoing arrows, the flow would dead-end. Diamonds always have arrows leaving.

questions.text: A flowchart and a piece of pseudocode for the same task:

answers.text: Are completely different algorithms
answers.feedback: ❌ The same algorithm can be drawn OR written. The form is different; the algorithm is the same.

answers.text: Are two different ways to express the same algorithm
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Flowchart, pseudocode, and real code are three forms of the SAME algorithm. (SC.K12.CTR.3.1)

answers.text: Cannot be translated between each other
answers.feedback: ❌ They CAN be translated — that's a major skill of programming.

answers.text: Mean different things to a computer when run
answers.feedback: ❌ Neither flowchart nor pseudocode "runs." Real code runs. All three describe the same algorithm.

questions.text: What is the data type of True in Python?

answers.text: Integer (int)
answers.feedback: ❌ Integers are whole numbers. True is yes/no — that's a different type.

answers.text: String (str)

answers.text: Boolean (bool)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Booleans hold YES/NO, ON/OFF, TRUE/FALSE. True and False are the only two boolean values. (SC.6.PE.1.1)

answers.text: Float
answers.feedback: ❌ Floats are numbers with decimals (3.14, 2.0). True isn't a number.

questions.text: Which is the BEST example of the digital divide?

answers.text: Using a smartphone to text a friend
answers.feedback: ❌ Texting is using technology. The digital divide is about UNEQUAL ACCESS to technology.

answers.text: Some students having reliable home internet while others don't
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The digital divide is the gap between people who have reliable access to technology (especially internet) and people who don't. (SC.6.PE.1.3)

answers.text: The difference between Apple and Android operating systems
answers.feedback: ❌ Apple vs Android is platform choice — both are widely available. Digital divide is about access, not preference.

answers.text: A new computer being faster than an old computer
answers.feedback: ❌ Speed differences happen but aren't the digital divide. The divide is about who has access at all.

questions.text: In Python, what does the == operator do (note: this is different from =)?

answers.text: Compares two values for equality and returns True or False
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! == asks "are these two equal?" and returns True or False. (SC.6.PE.1.4)

answers.text: Adds two numbers together
answers.feedback: ❌ + adds. == compares.

answers.text: Divides one number by another

answers.text: Nothing prints

questions.text: When TikTok shows you an endless feed of recommended videos, what core programming concept is at work?

answers.text: A flowchart drawn by an artist for each user

answers.feedback: ❌ Debuggers find bugs — they don't generate feeds. The feed itself is built with a loop.

questions.text: The Python statement if x = 5: causes the program to refuse to run at all (Python won't even start). What KIND of bug is this?

answers.text: Logic error — the math is wrong
answers.feedback: ❌ A logic error means the code runs but gets the wrong answer. Here the program refuses to RUN — that's a different kind of bug.

answers.text: Runtime error — happens only sometimes when the program runs
answers.feedback: ❌ Runtime errors happen DURING execution. Here the program won't even start — Python catches the bug before it runs.

answers.text: Syntax error — the line breaks Python's grammar rules
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Inside an if, Python expects a comparison (==), not an assignment (=). That's a grammar/syntax violation, caught BEFORE the program runs. (SC.6.PE.3.5)

answers.text: Network error — the internet is down
answers.feedback: ❌ This bug is in the code, not the network. Network errors are about connectivity, not syntax.

questions.text: Which of the following BEST describes a digital model?

answers.text: An exact, perfect copy of something real, with every detail included
answers.feedback: ❌ A model is simplified, not perfect — that's the whole point. A perfect copy would be the real thing, not a model.

answers.text: A simplified version of something real, built from numbers and rules so we can study or predict it
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A digital model is a simplified version of something real, built from numbers and rules so we can study or predict it. (SC.6.PE.3.1)

answers.text: Any photograph saved on a computer
answers.feedback: ❌ A photo is a static image. A model is something you can run, change, and use to predict behavior.

answers.text: A piece of computer hardware shaped like the thing it represents
answers.feedback: ❌ Digital models are made of code, numbers, and rules — not physical hardware shaped like the subject.

questions.text: You are building a model that predicts how long a snowman will last on a sunny day. Which is the BEST example of a variable in this model?

answers.text: The freezing point of water (0°C)
answers.feedback: ❌ The freezing point of water is a constant — it doesn't change. A variable is something that can change.

answers.text: Outside temperature, which changes by hour and by day
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Outside temperature changes — that's exactly what a variable is. The model checks the variable to predict how fast the snowman melts. (SC.6.PE.3.1)

answers.text: The number of pi (π)
answers.feedback: ❌ π is a mathematical constant — it never changes. Variables are values that can change inside a model.

answers.text: The standard chemical formula for water (H₂O)
answers.feedback: ❌ A chemical formula is a fixed fact, not a value that changes during the simulation.

questions.text: Engineers run simulations of new airplane designs before building real planes. Which is the BEST reason for doing that?

answers.text: Building real planes is illegal until a simulation is done
answers.feedback: ❌ Building real planes isn't illegal — engineers do build and test them. The point is that simulations let them try ideas first, cheaply and safely.

answers.text: Simulations let engineers test many designs cheaply and safely, without risking real planes, time, or lives
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The big value of simulation is the safe, cheap "what if?" — you can explore many designs without committing real time, money, or lives. (SC.6.ET.1.1)

answers.text: Simulations always predict the future perfectly
answers.feedback: ❌ Simulations are powerful but never perfect. They're useful precisely because they help us prepare, not because they predict everything.

answers.text: Real planes don't work as well as simulated ones
answers.feedback: ❌ Real planes are the goal — simulations are just a step on the way. The reason for simulating first is risk and cost reduction.

questions.text: Which of these is an example of haptic feedback?

answers.text: A bright color on a screen
answers.feedback: ❌ Color is visual feedback. Haptic feedback is something you feel — usually a vibration or motion.

answers.text: A loud sound from speakers
answers.feedback: ❌ Sound is auditory feedback, not haptic. Haptic = touch / feel.

answers.text: Your phone vibrating to alert you to a new message
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A vibration is haptic feedback — information you feel through your sense of touch. (SC.6.ET.1.1)

answers.text: A spoken voice from a smart speaker
answers.feedback: ❌ A spoken voice is auditory output. Haptic feedback is felt through touch, not heard.

questions.text: You're building a model of city traffic to help reduce rush-hour jams. Which detail is BEST to abstract away (leave out)?

answers.text: The number of cars entering each highway each minute
answers.feedback: ❌ Cars per minute is one of the most important variables for traffic — you'd never abstract that away.

answers.text: The average speed limit on each road
answers.feedback: ❌ Speed limits directly affect how fast traffic moves. Definitely keep this in the model.

answers.text: The exact paint color of each car
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Paint color doesn't change how traffic flows — that's exactly the kind of detail a good model abstracts away. (SC.6.PE.3.1)

answers.text: The location of major intersections
answers.feedback: ❌ Intersections are where jams form. The model needs to know where they are.

questions.text: Which of the following lists the five steps of the engineering design process in the correct order?

answers.text: Build a prototype → Identify the need → Research → Improve → Develop solutions
answers.feedback: ❌ You can't build a prototype before you know what problem you're solving. The process always starts by identifying the need.

answers.text: Identify the need → Research → Develop solutions → Build a prototype and test → Gather feedback and improve
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The five steps are: identify the need → research → develop solutions → build a prototype and test → gather feedback and improve. The cycle then loops back. (SC.6.PE.3.2)

answers.text: Research → Identify the need → Test → Develop solutions → Improve
answers.feedback: ❌ Research can't come before you know what to research. You have to identify the need first.

answers.text: Improve → Test → Develop → Research → Identify the need
answers.feedback: ❌ That's the order reversed. The cycle starts with identifying the need; you can't improve a design before it exists.

questions.text: A class is designing a robot that must reach the end of a maze in under 90 seconds and must be built using only the parts in the school's robotics kit. Which statement is BEST?

answers.text: Both rules are criteria — they describe what success looks like.
answers.feedback: ❌ Not quite. Criteria describe what success looks like; constraints are limits you can't cross. The parts-kit rule is a limit, not a goal.

answers.text: The 90-second time limit is a criterion (success goal); the parts-kit rule is a constraint (a limit).
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! "Reach the end in under 90 seconds" is the success goal — that's a criterion. "Use only the school's robotics kit" is a hard limit you can't cross — that's a constraint. (SC.6.PE.3.2)

answers.text: Both rules are constraints — they're both limits.
answers.feedback: ❌ The 90-second rule is the goal, not a limit. Goals are criteria; limits are constraints. The two rules play different roles.

answers.text: The parts-kit rule is a criterion, and the time limit is a constraint.
answers.feedback: ❌ Reversed. The 90-second rule defines success (criterion); the parts-kit rule limits how you may build (constraint).

questions.text: Which statement BEST describes iteration in the engineering design process?

answers.text: Doing the design once and never changing it.
answers.feedback: ❌ Almost no real design is finished on the first try. Doing it once is the opposite of iteration.

answers.text: Starting over from scratch every time, with no memory of past attempts.
answers.feedback: ❌ Iteration carries lessons forward — that's the whole point. Starting over with no memory wastes the feedback you collected.

answers.text: Going around the design cycle again, using what you learned last time to make the next version better.
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Iteration means looping the cycle again with what you learned last time. Each iteration should make the design better. (SC.6.PE.3.3)

answers.text: A sign of failure that good engineers avoid.
answers.feedback: ❌ Iteration is the opposite of failure — it's how excellence is actually built. Real engineers iterate on purpose.

questions.text: Your team has a working video-game prototype. The team has played it and it runs fine, but no one outside the team has ever tried it. What is the BEST next step in the design process?

answers.text: Declare the prototype final — if the team likes it, it's ready.
answers.feedback: ❌ The team built it — of course they like it. The point of testing is to expose the design to people who didn't build it.

answers.text: Add 30 more features before showing anyone the game.
answers.feedback: ❌ Adding features without testing what you have just buries the bugs deeper. Test first, then improve.

answers.text: Get external testers to play it, gather feedback, and use that feedback to improve the design.
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Step 4–5 of the cycle: get external testers, gather feedback, and improve. A working prototype is exactly when external testing is most valuable. (SC.6.PE.3.3)

answers.text: Throw the prototype away and start a different game.
answers.feedback: ❌ A working prototype is a victory — don't throw it out before you've even tested it. Iterate on what you have first.

questions.text: A teammate says: "Our design works perfectly on the first try. We don't need to test it or change it — it's already finished." Which response is BEST, based on the engineering design process?

answers.text: Agree — if it works, it's done.
answers.feedback: ❌ "Works for us" almost never means "works for everyone." The team built it, so they know how to use it. Real users will surprise you.

answers.text: Even a "finished" design usually needs more testing and iteration. Getting outside feedback almost always reveals problems we can't see ourselves.
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The fifth step of the cycle exists precisely because designs that look "finished" almost always have problems the designers can't see. Iteration is a virtue, not a sign of failure. (SC.6.PE.3.3)

answers.text: Agree, but only if no one has complained yet.
answers.feedback: ❌ "No one has complained" usually just means no one has tested it. Silence isn't proof of success.

answers.text: Disagree, and throw the design out completely just to be safe.
answers.feedback: ❌ Trashing the whole design without testing is just as wasteful as shipping it without testing. The right move is to gather feedback and iterate.

questions.text: Which of the following is a real use of AI you've probably already encountered?

questions.text: Which is a uniquely human strength that AI does not match well?

answers.text: Empathy and ethical judgment in unfamiliar situations

answers.text: Spotting tiny patterns in millions of data points
answers.feedback: ❌ Pattern matching at huge scale is a machine strength.

answers.text: Operating 24 hours a day without rest

questions.text: Which is a machine strength humans cannot match alone?

answers.text: Reading thousands of pages and finding one specific phrase in a fraction of a second

answers.text: Resolving a moral dilemma between two friends

answers.text: Inventing a new birthday tradition for your family

questions.text: "Human-in-the-loop" means a human stays involved in a decision the AI participates in. Which scenario most clearly requires human-in-the-loop?

answers.text: An auto-correct feature suggesting word fixes
answers.feedback: ❌ Auto-correct is a low-stakes suggestion you can accept or ignore — fine for automation.

answers.text: A music app shuffling your playlist
answers.feedback: ❌ Shuffling a playlist is low-stakes — automation is fine.

questions.text: An AI tool offers to write your friend's college essay. They ask if they should use it. What's the most prudent response?

answers.text: Yes — it's faster and easier; what could go wrong?
answers.feedback: ❌ Prudence asks "what could go wrong?" — the friend could face dishonesty consequences and lose the chance to learn from doing the work.

answers.text: Encourage them to write it themselves so the essay shows their real thinking — a college admissions reader is trying to learn about
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Prudence (wise foresight) recognizes that the essay's whole point is to share the friend's thinking. (SC.6.ET.3.2)

answers.text: Yes, but only if they remove the AI's name from the file
answers.feedback: ❌ Hiding the source doesn't change the deeper issue — the essay isn't actually their work.

answers.text: Don't say anything; it's not your problem
answers.feedback: ❌ Silence isn't prudence. A good friend offers honest, careful counsel.

questions.text: Which of the following BEST describes machine learning?

answers.text: A programmer types in every rule the software needs to follow, by hand
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes traditional programming, not machine learning. Machine learning is special because the rules come from patterns in data, not from a programmer typing them in.

answers.text: Software that improves at a task by being shown lots of examples (training data) instead of being given hand-written rules
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Machine learning is software that gets better at a task by being shown lots of examples — it learns the pattern from data instead of being told the rules. (SC.6.ET.2.1)

answers.text: A robot that physically learns by walking around a classroom
answers.feedback: ❌ Machine learning isn't about a physical robot — it's about how the software inside is built. It "learns" from data, not from walking around.

answers.text: Any program that runs on a fast computer
answers.feedback: ❌ Speed alone doesn't make a program AI. The defining trait of machine learning is that it adjusts itself based on examples.

questions.text: Which of these is BEST described as learning-based software (rather than rules-based)?

answers.text: A microwave that runs for exactly 30 seconds when you press "30 sec"
answers.feedback: ❌ A microwave timer is rules-based — it follows a fixed countdown. It doesn't learn from how you've used it before.

answers.text: A traffic light cycling green-yellow-red on a fixed timer
answers.feedback: ❌ A timed traffic light is rules-based — the schedule is fixed by humans. It doesn't adjust itself to traffic patterns it observes.

answers.text: A streaming app that recommends your next show based on what you and people like you have watched
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A recommender uses your past behavior — and patterns from millions of other users — to predict what you'll like next. That's classic learning-based AI. (SC.6.ET.2.1)

answers.text: A calculator computing 7 × 8
answers.feedback: ❌ A calculator is rules-based — 7 × 8 always equals 56. It doesn't get better at multiplication after a million uses.

questions.text: Which of these everyday tools is the BEST example of a generative AI?

answers.text: A chatbot that writes a brand-new poem about your dog when you ask it to
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Generative AI creates new text, images, audio, or video by predicting what should come next based on training data. A chatbot writing a poem is a textbook case. (SC.6.ET.2.1)

answers.text: A pocket calculator
answers.feedback: ❌ A calculator follows fixed math rules. It doesn't generate anything new — it computes a known answer.

answers.text: A digital clock
answers.feedback: ❌ A digital clock just displays the current time. No learning, no generation — just a counter.

answers.text: A flashlight app that turns the camera light on and off
answers.feedback: ❌ A flashlight app is rules-based: tap = on, tap = off. No AI involved.

questions.text: A company's AI hiring tool consistently rejects qualified women applicants. The team realizes the model was trained mostly on past hires — who were mostly men. What is this an example of, and what's the BEST first step?

answers.text: It's an example of an AI being "objective" — there's nothing to fix
answers.feedback: ❌ An AI that copies an unfair pattern is not objective — it's biased. "Objective" describes the math, not the outcome.

answers.text: It's an example of
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Bias from biased training data is a textbook AI ethics problem. The fix is to identify the bias, retrain on better data, and keep a human in the loop. (SC.6.ET.2.2)

answers.text: It's a privacy problem — the AI shouldn't see résumés at all
answers.feedback: ❌ Privacy is a real AI concern, but the issue here is different — the AI is making unfair decisions because of biased data, not because of who can see the résumés.

answers.text: It's an ownership problem — someone owns the wrong résumés
answers.feedback: ❌ Ownership is about who controls a creation. This problem is about fairness in how the AI evaluates people — that's bias.

questions.text: Late at night, your friend asks: "Can I just feed your essay into ChatGPT and have it write mine in the same style? Tomorrow's the deadline." Using Socratic / virtue-ethics reasoning — especially prudence — what is the BEST response?

answers.text: Send the essay without comment — friends help friends
answers.feedback: ❌ Prudence asks you to think past the next moment — the consequences for your friend, for you, for the teacher's trust. "Friends help friends" doesn't include helping each other cheat.

answers.text: Yell at them and refuse to talk to them again
answers.feedback: ❌ Prudence and friendship aren't opposites. You can decline AND be kind. Anger isn't a virtue here.

answers.text: Decline kindly, name the integrity issue, and offer to help them outline their own essay even though it's late
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! That's prudence, justice, and friendship working together — naming the issue, declining the shortcut, AND offering real help. Exactly the kind of choice the cardinal virtues point toward. (SC.6.ET.2.2)

answers.text: Use ChatGPT to write your friend's essay for them yourself, so at least you control the result
answers.feedback: ❌ Doing the cheating yourself doesn't fix the problem — it just transfers the dishonesty from your friend to you. Prudence rules that out too.

questions.text: (Week 29 review) A digital model of a pond uses sliders for rainfall, sun, and temperature, and shows water level and fish count changing in response. The sliders represent the model's:

answers.text: Outputs — what the model produces
answers.feedback: ❌ The water level and fish count are the outputs — what the model produces. The sliders are the inputs you control.

answers.text: Variables — values that can change to see how the model responds
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Sliders let the user change values — that's the textbook definition of a variable. (SC.6.PE.3.1)

answers.text: Constants — values that never change
answers.feedback: ❌ Constants don't change — sliders are designed precisely to let values change.

answers.text: Conditions — IF/THEN rules
answers.feedback: ❌ Conditions are the IF/THEN rules wired into the model. The sliders feed values into those rules but aren't the rules themselves.

questions.text: (Week 30 review) Your team has built a working prototype of a school-bus tracking app and three students have used it for a week. They report it crashes when they switch from Wi-Fi to cellular data. What is the BEST next step in the engineering design process?

answers.text: Ship it — three users isn't a lot of testers
answers.feedback: ❌ Shipping a known-broken product isn't engineering — it's hoping. The whole point of a prototype is to find problems and fix them.

answers.text: Use the feedback to revise and iterate — fix the crash and test again
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The "Test" stage feeds straight into "Improve" — gather feedback, fix the crash, test again. That's iteration. (SC.6.PE.3.2)

answers.text: Scrap the project entirely
answers.feedback: ❌ A working prototype with one fixable bug isn't a failed project. Iteration is meant for exactly this.

answers.text: Ignore the feedback — design choices belong to the team, not testers
answers.feedback: ❌ Real testers found a real bug. Ignoring user feedback skips the most valuable step in the design cycle.

questions.text: (Week 31 review) Which task is BEST suited for a machine working alone, with little or no human in the loop?

answers.text: Deciding whether to grant someone parole
answers.feedback: ❌ Parole decisions are high-stakes ethical judgments — they require a human in the loop, not a fully automated machine.

answers.text: Sorting 500,000 photos by which contain a cat
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! High-volume, low-judgment pattern recognition is exactly where machines shine on their own. (SC.6.ET.3.2)

answers.text: Comforting a grieving family member
answers.feedback: ❌ Comforting someone takes empathy — a uniquely human strength. Outsourcing this to a machine wouldn't be kind.

answers.text: Diagnosing a complicated medical case
answers.feedback: ❌ Complicated medical cases use AI tools to assist — but a human doctor remains in the loop. This is collaboration, not solo machine work.

questions.text: (Week 32 review) A friend tells you they used an AI tool to write their entire history essay and submitted it as their own work. Which response BEST reflects the cardinal virtue of fortitude?

answers.text: Use AI for your own essay too — it's faster
answers.feedback: ❌ Doing the same shortcut isn't fortitude — it's giving up on the harder, more rewarding path.

answers.text: Say nothing and let them deal with it
answers.feedback: ❌ Silence may feel safer, but it's not fortitude. Fortitude shows up in your own choices first.

answers.text: Choose to write your own essay — even though it's harder — because doing the hard work is part of becoming a better writer
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Fortitude = persevering through hard work even when an easier path is available. Choosing to do your own writing is the virtue at work. (SC.6.ET.2.2)

answers.text: Report them anonymously without ever talking to them first
answers.feedback: ❌ Reporting without talking first might be motivated by something — but it isn't an example of fortitude as a virtue you practice on yourself.

questions.text: (Synthesis) Which statement BEST captures how learning-based AI relates to the digital models you studied in Week 29?

answers.text: Learning-based AI has no connection to digital models
answers.feedback: ❌ The connection is the whole point of Section 3 of this week's reading — learning-based AI is a kind of model.

answers.text: A learning-based AI is a digital model whose conditions were learned from data instead of written by hand
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Both have variables and produce outputs. The difference is just where the conditions came from — written vs learned. (SC.6.PE.3.1, SC.6.ET.2.1)

answers.text: Learning-based AI replaces all earlier kinds of digital models
answers.feedback: ❌ Rules-based models still outperform learning-based ones for many tasks (calculators, thermostats, traffic lights). They coexist.

answers.text: Digital models cannot have variables; only AI does
answers.feedback: ❌ Variables are foundational to all digital models, including the rules-based ones from Week 29.

questions.text: A simulation is BEST described as:

answers.text: A wild guess about what might happen
answers.feedback: ❌ Simulations are not guesses — they're structured runs of a model with rules and variables.

answers.text: What happens when a digital model is run and shows how it behaves over time or under different inputs
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A simulation is the running of a digital model. (SC.6.PE.3.1)

answers.text: A static picture stored on a computer
answers.feedback: ❌ Static images don't change. Simulations show change over time or under different inputs.

answers.text: A list of facts about something real
answers.feedback: ❌ A list of facts is just data. A simulation runs rules over data and produces new behavior.

questions.text: Which of these is an example of a condition in a digital model?

answers.text: score = 0
answers.feedback: ❌ That's a variable being given a starting value, not a condition. Conditions are IF/THEN rules.

answers.text: IF score > 100 THEN level up
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! An IF/THEN rule is the textbook example of a condition. (SC.6.PE.3.1)

answers.text: player_name = "Alex"
answers.feedback: ❌ Setting a variable to a string is just an assignment, not a condition.

answers.text: lives = 3
answers.feedback: ❌ Another variable assignment, not a condition. Conditions check something with IF.

questions.text: When a game controller buzzes after your character takes damage, that is an example of:

answers.text: Gesture tracking
answers.feedback: ❌ Gesture tracking reads body or hand motion. The buzz is something you feel, not motion you make.

answers.text: Voice input
answers.feedback: ❌ Voice input is spoken commands. A controller buzz is felt, not heard.

answers.text: Haptic feedback
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Haptic feedback is information you feel through vibration or motion. (SC.6.ET.1.1)

answers.text: Typing on a keyboard
answers.feedback: ❌ Typing is text input. Haptic feedback is felt through your sense of touch.

questions.text: Which step comes FIRST in the engineering design process?

answers.text: Build a prototype
answers.feedback: ❌ You need to know what problem you're solving before you start building. Prototypes come later.

answers.text: Identify the need or problem
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Identifying the need/problem comes first. The whole rest of the cycle depends on naming what you're solving. (SC.6.PE.3.2)

answers.text: Test the design with users
answers.feedback: ❌ Testing happens after a prototype exists, which happens after the problem is identified.

answers.text: Improve the design
answers.feedback: ❌ Improving requires that something has been tested first. That's much later in the cycle.

questions.text: Your design team has $50 to spend on parts. This $50 limit is BEST described as a:

answers.text: Criterion (a measure of success)
answers.feedback: ❌ A criterion measures whether the design works (e.g., "must support 5 kg"). A budget cap is a limit, not a success measure.

answers.text: Constraint (a limit you must work within)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A budget limit constrains what you can do — that's a constraint. (SC.6.PE.3.3)

answers.text: Prototype
answers.feedback: ❌ A prototype is a working draft of the design itself, not a budget limit.

answers.text: Iteration
answers.feedback: ❌ Iteration is going around the design cycle again. Not a description of a $50 cap.

questions.text: You test your prototype, find a real bug, and now must decide what to do. Which response BEST reflects the design process?

answers.text: Ship the buggy version anyway
answers.feedback: ❌ Shipping known bugs isn't engineering — it's hoping. The whole point of testing is to find issues so you can fix them.

answers.text: Throw away all your work and start completely from scratch
answers.feedback: ❌ One bug rarely justifies starting over. Iteration means refining what you have, not throwing it away.

answers.text: Revise the design to fix the bug, then test again — iterate
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The Test → Improve loop is the engine of design. Iteration takes you from rough draft to polished work. (SC.6.PE.3.3)

answers.text: Hide the bug from your testers
answers.feedback: ❌ Hiding a real bug fails your users. Honesty about what works and what doesn't is part of good design.

questions.text: Which of these tasks plays to a uniquely human strength that machines do not match?

answers.text: Sorting one million photos by which contain a cat
answers.feedback: ❌ Pattern recognition at huge scale is a machine strength.

answers.text: Comforting a friend whose pet just died
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Empathy in real grief is uniquely human. (SC.6.ET.3.2)

answers.text: Multiplying two six-digit numbers in under a second
answers.feedback: ❌ Calculators have done that since the 1970s — pure machine strength.

answers.text: Spotting fraud across thousands of credit-card transactions per second
answers.feedback: ❌ Machines do this in milliseconds. Humans can't keep up at that scale.

questions.text: Which of these tasks plays to a machine strength that humans cannot match alone?

answers.text: Choosing the right comforting words for a frightened child
answers.feedback: ❌ Empathy and tone in real-time emotional support are human strengths.

answers.text: Scanning thousands of medical images per second to flag suspicious spots
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! High-volume pattern recognition at speed is exactly where machines outperform humans. (SC.6.ET.3.2)

answers.text: Deciding whether a parolee should be released
answers.feedback: ❌ Parole is high-stakes ethical judgment — must keep a human in the loop.

answers.text: Resolving a moral dilemma about loyalty between two friends
answers.feedback: ❌ Moral dilemmas about relationships are deeply human territory.

questions.text: Which of the following tasks most clearly requires a human in the loop, not a fully automated machine?

answers.text: Sorting thumbnails of vacation photos
answers.feedback: ❌ Low-stakes, repetitive sorting is fine for machines.

answers.text: A fitness watch counting daily steps
answers.feedback: ❌ A step counter is a simple sensor + math — automation is exactly right for this.

answers.text: Deciding whether someone is hired for a teaching job
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Hiring decisions affect people's lives and have a history of biased automation. A human must stay in the loop. (SC.6.ET.3.2)

answers.text: Adding up the total cost of items in a shopping cart
answers.feedback: ❌ Adding up totals is straightforward arithmetic — no human judgment needed.

questions.text: A simple calculator computing 9 + 5 is BEST described as:

answers.text: Learning-based software that improves with each calculation
answers.feedback: ❌ A calculator doesn't improve from data. The math operations are fixed.

answers.text: Rules-based software that follows fixed instructions
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A calculator runs hand-written rules for math. Nothing about it learns. (SC.6.ET.2.1)

answers.text: Generative AI
answers.feedback: ❌ Generative AI creates new content. A calculator isn't generative — it gives one fixed answer.

answers.text: A trained machine learning model
answers.feedback: ❌ Machine learning models train on data. A basic calculator doesn't.

questions.text: Machine learning is BEST described as:

answers.text: Software that follows pre-written rules typed in by a programmer
answers.feedback: ❌ That describes RULES-BASED software, not learning-based. The whole difference is whether the rules came from data or a human.

answers.text: Software that improves itself by spotting patterns in data
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Machine learning systems get better by training on data instead of being told every rule. (SC.6.ET.2.1)

answers.text: A team of human teachers who write code together
answers.feedback: ❌ Machine learning is software, not a group of teachers.

answers.text: Hardware that can read minds
answers.feedback: ❌ ML doesn't read minds. It looks for statistical patterns in data you give it.

questions.text: An AI hiring tool keeps unfairly rejecting qualified women applicants. Where did this bias most likely come from?

answers.text: The brand of laptop the AI runs on
answers.feedback: ❌ Hardware brand has nothing to do with bias.

answers.text: The training data — historical hiring records were already biased, so the AI learned the bias
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Bias in AI almost always comes from biased training data. The model is only as just as the data that taught it. (SC.6.ET.2.2)

answers.text: The time of day the candidate applied
answers.feedback: ❌ Time of day isn't where bias enters the system.

answers.text: A magic property of computers
answers.feedback: ❌ There's no magic — bias has a clear cause: the data used to train the model.

questions.text: You set a daily limit on social-media scrolling so the recommendation algorithm doesn't keep you up past midnight. Which cardinal virtue does this BEST reflect?

answers.text: Prudence
answers.feedback: ❌ Prudence is wise foresight — it could be involved, but the specific virtue of moderating use is temperance.

answers.text: Justice
answers.feedback: ❌ Justice is about fairness toward others. Limiting your own scrolling is about restraining yourself.

answers.text: Fortitude
answers.feedback: ❌ Fortitude is perseverance through hard work. This isn't about persevering — it's about restraining excess.

answers.text: Temperance
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Temperance is the virtue of moderation — choosing the right amount, not the maximum amount. (SC.6.ET.2.2)

questions.text: Which statement BEST captures the big idea of Unit 4?

answers.text: AI will replace humans in every task in the next decade
answers.feedback: ❌ Unit 4 made the opposite case — humans bring strengths machines don't, and high-stakes calls keep a human in the loop.

answers.text: Modeling, design, and AI are powerful tools that work best when guided by human judgment and the cardinal virtues
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The whole arc of Unit 4 was: powerful tools + human virtues = wise use. (All Unit 4 standards)

answers.text: The cardinal virtues have nothing to do with technology
answers.feedback: ❌ Unit 4 spent significant time linking the cardinal virtues to ethical use of technology — the connection is the point.

answers.text: Digital simulations always perfectly replace real-world testing
answers.feedback: ❌ Simulations are useful but never perfect — they help us prepare; real-world testing still matters.

questions.text: Which statement BEST describes a learning-based AI?

answers.text: It is magical and impossible to understand
answers.feedback: ❌ Learning-based AI has clear, explainable mechanics — it's a model trained on data.

answers.text: It is software with no rules at all
answers.feedback: ❌ Learning-based AI does have rules — they were just learned from data, not typed by hand.

answers.text: It is a digital model whose conditions were learned from data, not handwritten by a programmer
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A learning-based AI is just a digital model where the conditions came from training data instead of being handwritten. (SC.6.PE.3.1, SC.6.ET.2.1)

answers.text: It is a piece of physical hardware
answers.feedback: ❌ AI is software, not hardware. It runs on hardware but it isn't itself a physical thing.

quizzes.title: Week 35 Quiz — Careers in Computing & Digital Citizenship

questions.text: Maria's job is to make sure that when you tap a button in an app, it feels right — that the layout, color, words, and flow guide you naturally and work for people with all kinds of abilities. Which CS career is Maria MOST likely in?

answers.text: Cybersecurity analyst
answers.feedback: ❌ Cybersecurity analysts protect systems from attack. Maria's work is about how the app feels, not defense.

answers.text: UX designer
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! UX designers shape how a product feels and flows for the people using it — including making it accessible. (SC.6.ET.1.2)

answers.text: Data scientist
answers.feedback: ❌ Data scientists find patterns in big data sets. Maria's focus is the user experience, not the data.

answers.text: Network administrator
answers.feedback: ❌ Network admins keep computers and Wi-Fi connected. That's important work, but it's not about how apps feel to use.

questions.text: Daniela never finished college. Over four years she taught herself to code, built a public portfolio of real projects, and contributed to open-source software. Which statement about her chances of becoming a software engineer is MOST accurate?

answers.text: It's impossible — every software engineer must have a four-year CS degree
answers.feedback: ❌ This is a common myth. Many software engineers came in through bootcamps, self-teaching, or apprenticeships.

answers.text: Self-teaching with a strong portfolio of real projects is a recognized path into software engineering — many engineers came in this way
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Self-teaching with a real portfolio is a legitimate path — practice on real problems is the common thread across every route into CS. (SC.6.ET.1.2)

answers.text: Only a bootcamp counts — anything else is just a hobby
answers.feedback: ❌ Bootcamps are one good path, but they're not the only one. Self-teaching, apprenticeship, and the degree path all work.

answers.text: She'll have to start over from scratch with a brand-new four-year CS degree before anyone will consider her
answers.feedback: ❌ She doesn't have to start over. Many companies hire based on demonstrated skill — a polished portfolio is real evidence.

questions.text: You're a security engineer at a streaming company. You discover a critical bug that would let anyone steal user passwords. What is the MOST ethical FIRST move?

answers.text: Quietly sell the bug to whoever offers the most money
answers.feedback: ❌ Selling a vulnerability to attackers harms real users. That's a clear ethical failure.

answers.text: Post the exact bug publicly on social media before the company can react
answers.feedback: ❌ Public disclosure before a fix is in place actually exposes users to attackers. Responsible disclosure goes to the company first.

answers.text: Report it to your security team and leadership immediately, then help patch it before users are harmed
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Report internally first, then help patch the bug before users are harmed. This is responsible disclosure — the ethical heart of cybersecurity. (SC.6.TI.2.1)

answers.text: Wait a year to see if anyone else finds it first
answers.feedback: ❌ Waiting just leaves users exposed. Speed protects people; hesitation harms them.

questions.text: A classmate posts a video of themselves tripping and spilling lunch everywhere. Comments are piling up making fun of them. What is the MOST PRUDENT response, in the classical sense of prudence (wise foresight)?

answers.text: Pile on with a clever joke — everyone else is doing it
answers.feedback: ❌ Piling on harms a real person for a small social reward. Prudence pauses before the joke.

answers.text: Screenshot and share to a group chat so even more people see it
answers.feedback: ❌ Amplifying someone's bad day is the opposite of prudence — it makes the harm bigger.

answers.text: Don't pile on. If it feels right, send the person a private message that's kind
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Prudence is the pause before publishing — and a small private kindness is justice in action. (SC.6.TI.1.1)

answers.text: Tell yourself it's "just the internet" and leave a sneaky negative emoji
answers.feedback: ❌ A "sneaky" negative reaction still adds harm. Prudence asks whether the click helps a real person — not whether it can be hidden.

questions.text: You feel like scrolling for another hour, but you're tired and have homework. You put the phone down. Which of the four cardinal virtues did you most clearly practice?

answers.text: Prudence — wise foresight
answers.feedback: ❌ Prudence is the pause before deciding. The act of stopping when you've had enough is closer to temperance.

answers.text: Justice — giving people what is owed
answers.feedback: ❌ Justice is about how you treat others. This choice was about how you treat yourself.

answers.text: Temperance — self-mastery, knowing what is enough
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Temperance is the virtue of knowing your limit and choosing it. Putting the phone down when enough is enough is temperance in action. (SC.6.TI.1.1)

answers.text: Fortitude — courage in hardship
answers.feedback: ❌ Fortitude does help, but the lead virtue here — knowing what is enough — is temperance.

questions.text: Which of the following is the BEST example of asynchronous communication?

answers.text: A live phone call
answers.feedback: ❌ A phone call is synchronous — both people must be there at the same time.

answers.text: A video chat with a classmate happening right now
answers.feedback: ❌ Video chat is synchronous — it happens live, in real time.

answers.text: An email you send tonight and your friend reads tomorrow morning
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Email is asynchronous — sender and reader don't have to be available at the same moment.

answers.text: Two people talking face to face in the same room
answers.feedback: ❌ Talking face to face is synchronous — both people are present at the same time.

questions.text: When you send a video clip to a friend across the internet, the data is MOST likely:

answers.text: Sent as one giant file along a single fixed path from your phone to theirs
answers.feedback: ❌ The internet doesn't use one big file along one fixed path — packets are far more flexible and reliable.

answers.text: Split into small chunks called packets that travel different paths and are reassembled at the destination
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Data is split into packets that hop between routers along different paths and reassemble at the destination. (Unit 1)

answers.text: Hand-carried by a network technician between buildings
answers.feedback: ❌ Network technicians don't hand-carry data — it travels electronically as packets.

answers.text: Stored only on your phone until your friend manually downloads it
answers.feedback: ❌ Sending is not just storage — the data moves across networks as packets, automatically.

questions.text: You send a friend a long, thoughtful message. They reply only "k." What's the MOST charitable way to handle it?

answers.text: Assume they're angry and stop talking to them
answers.feedback: ❌ Jumping to "they're angry" without checking is the trap text messages set. Ask first.

answers.text: Tone is hard to read in short texts — ask before assuming, or wait until you can talk in person
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Short texts strip out tone. The wise move is to check before assuming the worst. (Unit 1)

answers.text: Send "fine, bye then" and end the friendship
answers.feedback: ❌ Escalating in response to a one-letter reply is exactly the spiral good digital communication tries to avoid.

answers.text: Decide every "k." in the world definitely means hatred
answers.feedback: ❌ Texts are short and ambiguous — that's a feature, not a hidden code for hatred.

questions.text: You get an email that says "URGENT: your account is locked. Click here NOW to fix it." The link goes to a slightly misspelled version of your bank's web address. This is MOST likely:

answers.text: Your bank just changed its website name
answers.feedback: ❌ Banks don't change their web address by slightly misspelling it. That's a phishing red flag.

answers.text: A phishing attempt designed to steal your login and password
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Urgency + misspelled URL + "click NOW" is the classic phishing recipe. Don't click — open the real site directly. (Unit 2)

answers.text: A normal software update message
answers.feedback: ❌ Software updates don't come from outside emails pushing urgency and links to misspelled URLs.

answers.text: A friend playing a harmless joke
answers.feedback: ❌ Friends don't typically send fake bank lockout emails. This is a phishing pattern.

questions.text: Which is the STRONGEST password choice for a personal account?

answers.text: password123
answers.feedback: ❌ "password123" is on every list of cracked passwords. A bot would guess it in milliseconds.

answers.text: Your birthday
answers.feedback: ❌ Birthdays are easy for anyone who knows you (or scrapes social media) to guess.

answers.text: A long unique phrase you don't use on any other site
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Long + unique + not reused is the recipe for a strong password. (Unit 2)

answers.text: Your pet's name
answers.feedback: ❌ Pet names are often posted publicly. They're easy to find and easy to guess.

questions.text: You see a stranger online getting roasted in the comments for a small mistake. What's the BEST digital-citizen response?

answers.text: Pile on with a clever joke of your own
answers.feedback: ❌ Piling on harms a real person for a small social reward. Good digital citizenship pauses first.

answers.text: Screenshot it and post to your own feed
answers.feedback: ❌ Amplifying someone's bad day is the opposite of being a good digital citizen.

answers.text: Don't add to the harm — and if it feels right, defend or message kindly
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Don't add to the harm; if appropriate, defend or message kindly. That's digital citizenship in action. (Unit 2)

answers.text: Tag five friends to come laugh too
answers.feedback: ❌ Pulling more people into the pile-on is the opposite of what a good citizen does.

questions.text: In a program you write: score = 0. Later: score = score + 10. The score in this code is a:

answers.text: Function
answers.feedback: ❌ A function is a named reusable block of code. score is just a name holding a value.

answers.text: Loop
answers.feedback: ❌ A loop repeats a block of code. score doesn't repeat — it holds a value.

answers.text: Variable
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A variable is a named box that holds a value that can change. (Unit 3)

answers.text: Comment
answers.feedback: ❌ A comment is text the computer ignores. score is real code that the computer uses.

questions.text: A program contains: IF temperature > 32 THEN turn on cooler. The variable temperature equals 28. What does the program do?

answers.text: It turns the cooler on
answers.feedback: ❌ The condition requires temperature greater than 32. With temperature = 28, the IF is false.

answers.text: It does NOT turn the cooler on
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! 28 is not greater than 32, so the IF is false and the cooler stays off. (Unit 3)

answers.text: It changes the value of temperature to 32
answers.feedback: ❌ The IF only checks the value — it doesn't change it.

answers.text: It crashes
answers.feedback: ❌ There's nothing here to crash. A clean false IF just skips the THEN block.

questions.text: A loop in a program is MOST useful when you want to:

answers.text: Save the program for later
answers.feedback: ❌ Saving a program is what a file-save command does — not a loop.

answers.text: Repeat a block of code (a specific number of times, or for each item in a list)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Loops repeat code — a counted number of times, or once per item in a list. (Unit 3)

answers.text: Send a message to another computer
answers.feedback: ❌ That's networking. Loops are about repetition inside one program.

answers.text: Stop the program forever
answers.feedback: ❌ Loops don't stop programs — they repeat blocks of code.

questions.text: Your program crashes with an error message. What is the MOST productive first move?

answers.text: Delete the whole program and start over
answers.feedback: ❌ Deleting throws away every clue. Read first, fix second.

answers.text: Read the error message carefully — it usually tells you where to look
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! The error message is the program's letter to you. Read it — most of the answer is in it. (Unit 3)

answers.text: Run the same code again unchanged and hope for a different result
answers.feedback: ❌ Same code + same data = same crash. Read the error and change something.

answers.text: Blame the computer
answers.feedback: ❌ The computer is doing exactly what you wrote. The bug is almost always in the code, not the machine.

questions.text: A digital model is BEST described as:

answers.text: An exact, perfect copy of something real with every detail
answers.feedback: ❌ A model is simplified, not perfect — that's the whole point.

answers.text: A simplified version of something real, built from numbers and rules so we can study or predict it
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A digital model is numbers + rules, built to study or predict the real thing. (Unit 4)

answers.text: A photograph saved on a computer
answers.feedback: ❌ A photo is static. A model can be run and changed.

answers.text: A piece of hardware shaped like the thing it represents
answers.feedback: ❌ Digital models are code, not hardware shaped like an object.

questions.text: You're modeling how long a snowman lasts on a sunny day. Which is the BEST example of a variable in this model?

answers.text: The freezing point of water (0°C)
answers.feedback: ❌ The freezing point of water doesn't change — it's a constant.

answers.text: Outdoor temperature (changes hour by hour)
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Outdoor temperature changes hour by hour — that's exactly what a variable is. (Unit 4)

answers.text: The mathematical value of pi
answers.feedback: ❌ Pi is a mathematical constant — it never changes.

answers.text: The chemical formula for water (H₂O)
answers.feedback: ❌ A chemical formula is a fixed fact, not a value that changes during a simulation.

questions.text: Which step typically comes FIRST in the engineering design process?

answers.text: Build the final product
answers.feedback: ❌ Building comes much later. Engineering starts with understanding the problem.

answers.text: Identify the problem and define its criteria and constraints
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Define the problem and its criteria/constraints first. Everything else follows. (Unit 4 · Week 30)

answers.text: Run a final user test
answers.feedback: ❌ Testing comes after design and prototype. First you need a problem to solve.

answers.text: Ship the product and write the marketing copy
answers.feedback: ❌ Shipping is the last step, not the first.

questions.text: An AI system flags a patient as "high risk" for a serious illness. Following the human-in-the-loop principle, what should happen next?

answers.text: Treatment begins automatically based on the AI's flag
answers.feedback: ❌ Automatic treatment based on an AI flag removes the human from the loop — exactly what the principle says to avoid.

answers.text: A doctor reviews the flag, talks with the patient, and decides what to do
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! A human-in-the-loop design keeps a doctor accountable for the call — the AI assists, the doctor decides. (Unit 4)

answers.text: The patient is automatically emailed a diagnosis
answers.feedback: ❌ Auto-emailing a diagnosis skips the human conversation that real care requires.

answers.text: The AI's confidence score is trusted with no human review
answers.feedback: ❌ Trusting confidence scores with no review is the opposite of human-in-the-loop.

questions.text: A company builds an AI hiring tool by training it on past hiring decisions. The past hires were 90% from one demographic group. Which problem is MOST likely?

answers.text: The AI will perform perfectly because past data is always trustworthy
answers.feedback: ❌ Past data carries past biases. "Always trustworthy" is exactly the AI ethics warning sign.

answers.text: The AI may carry forward and amplify the bias of past decisions, treating new applicants unfairly
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Trained on biased history, an AI will repeat and amplify that bias — this is the textbook AI-ethics problem. (Unit 4)

answers.text: The AI will hire applicants completely at random
answers.feedback: ❌ A trained AI doesn't hire at random — it follows patterns it learned from the data.

answers.text: The AI will refuse to hire anyone at all
answers.feedback: ❌ A normally-trained AI doesn't refuse to hire — it carries the patterns of the data it was trained on.

questions.text: You're modeling traffic flow on a highway. Which detail is BEST to abstract away (leave out)?

answers.text: Cars per minute entering each ramp
answers.feedback: ❌ Cars-per-minute is one of the most important variables for traffic flow. Keep it.

answers.text: Number of lanes
answers.feedback: ❌ Number of lanes directly affects how much traffic the road can carry. Keep it.

answers.text: The paint color of each car
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Paint color doesn't affect traffic flow — it's exactly the kind of irrelevant detail abstraction removes. (Unit 4)

answers.text: Average speed limit on each road
answers.feedback: ❌ Speed limit directly affects how fast traffic moves. Keep it.

questions.text: Whose job is it to find patterns in large amounts of data to answer questions like "what's happening?" and "what might happen next?"

answers.text: Cybersecurity analyst
answers.feedback: ❌ Cybersecurity is about defense, not finding patterns in data sets to answer business questions.

answers.text: Data scientist
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Finding patterns in data and predicting "what might happen next" is the data scientist's calling. (Unit 5)

answers.text: UX designer
answers.feedback: ❌ UX designers shape how products feel to use — not data analysis.

answers.text: Network administrator
answers.feedback: ❌ Network admins keep computers and networks running — not the same as data analysis.

questions.text: Which statement about paths into a CS career is MOST accurate?

answers.text: Only a four-year CS degree leads to a real CS career
answers.feedback: ❌ This is a common myth. Many engineers came in through bootcamps, self-teaching, or apprenticeships.

answers.text: Multiple paths work — degree, bootcamp, self-teaching, apprenticeship — and the common thread is practice on real problems
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Multiple paths into CS exist, and the common thread is real practice on real problems. (Unit 5)

answers.text: You must start before age 10 to have any chance
answers.feedback: ❌ Lots of working engineers started after age 10 — even after age 30 or 40. Age is not the barrier.

answers.text: The internet age made it impossible for adults to learn CS
answers.feedback: ❌ The internet actually makes self-teaching easier than ever. Adults learn CS every day.

questions.text: A security engineer discovers a critical bug in their company's product. What is the MOST ethical FIRST move?

answers.text: Sell the bug secretly to the highest bidder
answers.feedback: ❌ Selling a vulnerability harms real users — a clear ethical failure.

answers.text: Post it publicly on social media before the company can react
answers.feedback: ❌ Public disclosure before a fix exposes users. Responsible disclosure goes to the company first.

answers.text: Report it internally and help patch it before users are harmed
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Responsible disclosure: report internally, then patch before users are harmed. (Unit 5)

answers.text: Use it to peek at colleagues' accounts
answers.feedback: ❌ Using a bug to snoop on coworkers is an abuse of trust. Don't do it.

questions.text: You feel like scrolling for another hour, but you're tired and have homework. You close the app and go finish your work. Which of the four cardinal virtues did you most clearly practice?

answers.text: Prudence — wise foresight
answers.feedback: ❌ Prudence is the pause before deciding. The act of stopping when you've had enough is closer to temperance.

answers.text: Justice — giving people what is owed
answers.feedback: ❌ Justice is about how you treat others. This choice was about how you treat yourself.

answers.text: Temperance — self-mastery, knowing what is enough
answers.feedback: ✅ Correct! Temperance is knowing your limit and choosing it. Putting the phone down when enough is enough is temperance in action. (Unit 5)

answers.text: Fortitude — courage in hardship
answers.feedback: ❌ Fortitude helps, but the lead virtue here — knowing what is enough — is temperance.
